attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter post.

semantics.note: 'I no longer believe the majority are doing anything other than collecting dust' is a firm present-state claim that most Blackwell GPUs sit unused in storage. It is not a probabilistic hedge, and the normalisation matches it.

contract.note: Taking the claim as more than half of shipped data-center Blackwell packages being unused in storage in May 2026 is an ordinary reading. Counting packages and excluding lightly used installed GPUs is fair. Because he also said 'warehouse', counting units in transit or staging as stored would be a judgement call.

evidence.note: Epoch says delivered chips may take time to come online. That is methodology only: it gives no May 2026 inventory and no share of chips in storage.

Estimates about 10% in staging at end-2025 by assuming earlier shipments were fully deployed. It points against his claim, but it covers a different period and rests on modelled assumptions rather than a reconciled inventory.

reviews.rationale: The contract needs a reconciled May 2026 count of shipments against storage status. The packet has none. Epoch only notes deployment lag, and American Compute's roughly 10% staging figure is a modelled end-2025 estimate. Neither establishes or refutes that most Blackwell packages were in warehouses in May 2026.

attribution.note: Zitron's own first-person statement in his post.

semantics.note: The normalisation keeps the personal-research qualifier ('he could find'), the 'few hundred megawatts' threshold and the two-year window.

contract.note: The contract reads the claim narrowly, as a report of his own search, so market-wide totals cannot contradict it. That is fair to his words, but it leaves the claim nearly untestable without a record of what he actually found. The choice of reading decides how evidence is weighed.

evidence.note: Microsoft says it added a gigawatt in one quarter. This is the company describing itself, and it says nothing about Zitron's research sample, so under the contract it cannot contradict the personal-research claim.

reviews.rationale: Scored as a claim about what his research found, it needs an independent record of the projects he identified. The packet has none. Microsoft's gigawatt figure is a company disclosure about a broader total and, under the contract, does not contradict the personal finding.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his post.

semantics.note: The 'will continue' clause has no subject of its own. It is joined to 'it's bonking' inside the 'suggests that' clause, so 'suggests' qualifies both parts. Splitting off a firm 'will' turns a tentative inference into a committed forecast. The antecedent is kept, but the hedge now covers less than it did.

contract.note: The contract treats the continuation as a firm conditional forecast, which is stricter than his hedged 'suggests'. It also has to supply its own definitions of 'subsidize' (subscription receipts below serving cost) and of a capacity constraint.

evidence.note: Anthropic's May 6, 2026 post, a company disclosure, announces higher limits and the SpaceX compute deal. It does not establish subscription subsidies, and it does not show capacity constraints ending.

reviews.rationale: The whole statement sits under 'suggests', which is hedged inference, so policy does not score it. Even on the drafter's split, there is no deadline, the subsidy antecedent is not established, and the packet shows no conclusive event. It would not be scored either way.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his post.

semantics.note: The core claim is a comparison: Microsoft's reported ~2GW against his ~342MW Fairwater estimate. 'Documented' overstates his self-described generous estimate, and the clause about rejecting the figure is adjacent rhetoric. Neither changes the testable comparison.

contract.note: Reading 'last six months' as the two reported quarters, and testing both inputs as well as the arithmetic, is fair. Whether the result counts as arithmetic only or as a physical comparison changes how much the outcome depends on the unverified denominator.

evidence.note: Microsoft reports nearly 1GW added in the December quarter. This confirms part of the reported numerator but does not verify it operationally.
Microsoft reports another gigawatt in the March quarter, so about 2GW was reported in total. 2000/342 is about 5.85, consistent with 'a little under six'. The 342MW denominator is not verified.

reviews.rationale: Microsoft's disclosures confirm it reported about 2GW, and the ratio to 342MW checks out at about 5.85. The contract also needs comparable records verifying the 342MW Fairwater figure and an operational reconciliation of the additions. Neither is in the packet, so the comparison cannot be settled.
